extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent owners, patent-office policymakers, and litigators considering effects of proposed U.S. patent-reform legislation
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes substantive legal/procedural standards and policy criteria from commentary on a proposed U.S. patent-reform bill (inter partes/post-grant proceedings, damages, estoppel, discovery, appeals, and related PTO practice). Useful for practitioners evaluating how to litigate, petition, or administer patents under the bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treble damages as deterrent to willful infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 284’s authorization of treble damages is designed to persuade companies that their best economic option is to respect valid patents; without treble damages many companies would find it economically rational to infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill preserves treble-damages awards’ role as a meaningful deterrent to reckless or wanton conduct, aiming for a standard that makes licensing the most economically reasonable option and deters copying.

rubrics_metrics.name: No adverse inference from failure to obtain/disclose opinion of counsel (Section 298)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adds new section 298 to title 35 barring courts and juries from drawing an adverse inference from an accused infringer’s failure to obtain an opinion of counsel as to infringement or his failure to waive privilege and disclose such an opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy choice protects attorney-client privilege and reduces pressure to obtain litigation-driven opinions; reflects legislative skepticism of the probative value of such opinions. Applies to findings of both willfulness and intent to induce infringement and legislatively abrogates Broadcom v. Qualcomm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion to adjudicative inter partes review with petitioner burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter partes reexamination is converted into an adjudicative proceeding (inter partes review) in which the petitioner, rather than the Office, bears the burden of showing unpatentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 316(e) assigns the petitioner the burden of proving unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence; the Office has discretion in prescribing regulations for the new proceeding, and will use that discretion to implement adjudicative procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes review availability expanded to all patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminates the bar on challenging pre-1999 patents in inter partes proceedings; removes requirement that an inter partes reexamination be terminated if litigation results in a final judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All patents can be challenged in inter partes review, and the proceeding will not automatically terminate upon a final judgment in related litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-grant review scope and estoppel limited to raised/decided issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Creates a post-grant review in which a patent can be challenged on any validity ground during the first nine months after issue; challengers who use this proceeding will be estopped in litigation from raising only those issues that were raised and decided in the post-grant review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with inter partes reexamination’s broader could-have-been-raised estoppel; post-grant estoppel only covers issues actually raised and decided during the proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Could-have-raised estoppel limited to 'reasonably' discoverable prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Softens the could-have-raised estoppel applied by inter partes review by adding the modifier 'reasonably,' so estoppel extends only to prior art that a skilled searcher reasonably could have been expected to discover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures estoppel does not extend to matters that would have required an impracticable worldwide 'scorched-earth' search; satisfaction of estoppel judged by what a diligent, skilled searcher would reasonably find.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of patent owner statements in claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Allows written statements of the patent owner regarding claim scope that have been filed in court or in the Office to be made part of the official file and to be considered in reexaminations and inter partes and post-grant reviews for purposes of claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps the Office understand and construe key claims and identify inconsistent statements where owners advocated broader scope in litigation than they urge in PTO proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes challenges limited to patents and printed publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Preserves the current scope of inter partes proceedings: only patents and printed publications may be used to challenge a patent in an inter partes review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintains limitation on prior art types usable in inter partes challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petitioners must disclose real parties in interest to patent owner
rubrics_metrics.description: Modified petition requirements (new sections 312(a)(5) and 322(a)(5)) require petitioners to provide to the patent owner the same identification of any real parties in interest or privies that is provided to the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipates that patent owners will investigate whether a petitioner is a real party in interest or a privy of a barred party; promotes transparency about who controls petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joinder of inter partes/post-grant reviews and Director factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 315(c) and 325(c) allow joinder of inter partes and post-grant reviews; Office anticipates joinder as of right for identical petitions but gives the Director discretion to allow or deny joinder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Director may consider factors such as differences in accused products/processes, breadth/unusualness of claim scope, claim-construction differences, number of patents/claims at issue, consent of patent owner, court requests, offers to pay patent-owner costs, and whether joinder petitions present additional challenges that meet institution thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director authority to reject repetitive or cumulative petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorizes the Director to reject any request for ex parte reexamination or petition for post-grant or inter partes review on the basis that the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments previously were presented to the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents parties from mounting repetitive or cumulative attacks that substantially overlap issues previously considered by the Office; if rejected due to numerical limits or overload the Office should indicate the basis for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel from raising issues in subsequent PTO proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (1) of sections 315(e) and 325(e) estops a party that uses inter partes or post-grant review from raising in a subsequent PTO proceeding any issue that he raised or reasonably could have raised in the post-grant or inter partes review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectively bars such parties (and their real parties in interest/privies) from later using inter partes review or ex parte reexamination to re-raise those issues; Office will need regulation changes to identify ex parte requesters to enforce this estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of estoppel to real parties in interest and privies (privity rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estoppels and other procedural limits are extended to real parties in interest and privies of the petitioner; privity is an equitable rule based on 'practical situation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether privity estoppel should extend to codefendants depends on fairness and whether patent owner has clearly and reliably identified asserted claims and constructions; Office may use joinder timing rules to mitigate unfairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery limits in inter partes and post-grant reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 316(a)(6) and 326(a)(5) prescribe discovery standards: in inter partes review discovery is limited to depositions of witnesses submitting affidavits/declarations and as otherwise necessary in the interest of justice; in post-grant review, discovery is broader but must be limited to evidence directly related to factual assertions advanced by either party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery is constrained to expedite proceedings while allowing necessary fact development, particularly in post-grant reviews that may raise issues (e.g., enablement, §101) needing factual development.

rubrics_metrics.name: 12-month completion deadline (plus 6-month extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 316(a)(12) and 326(a)(11) provide that inter partes and post-grant reviews must be completed within 12 months of institution, except the Office can extend the deadline by 6 months for good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is intended to drastically shorten typical multi-year inter partes reexaminations to a one-year target (plus limited extensions) by procedural reforms, elevated thresholds, and front-loading of petitioners' cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thresholds for instituting reviews: reasonable-likelihood and more-likely-than-not
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposes elevated thresholds for instituting proceedings: inter partes review employs a 'reasonable-likelihood-of-success' threshold; post-grant review uses a 'more-likely-than-not-invalidity' threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inter partes 'reasonable likelihood' requires petitioners to present a prima facie case justifying a rejection of the claims, assessed based on the petition and the patent owner’s response. Post-grant's higher threshold is intended for issues requiring factual development; ensures petitioners present a complete case at outset rather than relying on discovery to meet ultimate burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time bars for seeking reviews related to litigation (declaratory judgment and six-month rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 315(a) and 325(a) bar a party from seeking or maintaining review if he has filed a declaratory judgment action asserting patent invalidity; section 315(b) provides that if a party has been sued for infringement and wants inter partes review, he must do so within 6 months of being served with the infringement complaint (unless the petition is filed as a counterclaim scenario).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents forum-shopping and coordinates timing with civil litigation; different rules apply to accused infringers served with complaints versus parties that filed DJ actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-month rule protecting early patent-owner suits and injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 325(b) provides that if a patent owner sues to enforce his patent within three months after it is granted, a court cannot refuse to consider a motion for a preliminary injunction on the basis that a post-grant review has been requested or instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects market-participant patent owners who need injunctions to avoid irreparable harm during the early post-grant period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director authority to limit instituted reviews early and notice requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 5(c)(2)(C) and 5(f)(2) allow the Director to place a limit on the number of post-grant and inter partes reviews instituted during the first four years; if rejected due to this numerical limit, the Office should indicate the rejection was due to the limit and not on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory considerations under subsections (a)(2) and (b) of 316/326 require the Office to consider its ability to timely complete proceedings; safety valves to prevent backlog are expected and rejections for capacity reasons should be clearly explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety valve to decline institution if Office overwhelmed
rubrics_metrics.description: Under subsection (a)(2) and (b) of sections 316 and 326, the Office is required to implement thresholds via regulations and to consider its ability to timely complete proceedings, allowing the Office to decline institution if a high volume threatens timely completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferable to instituting proceedings that cannot be completed timely; rejections under this consideration should be distinguished from merit-based rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of intermediate BPAI appeals; direct Federal Circuit appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill eliminates intermediate administrative appeals of inter partes proceedings to the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences (BPAI), allowing parties to appeal only directly to the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduces two levels of appeal to one to accelerate resolution of inter partes cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on preissuance submissions (third-party only, first publication, USPTO publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 7 modifies preissuance submissions: only 'third party' (not 'person') may submit prior art; submissions are limited to the first publication (word 'first' added); and 'by the Office' was added to ensure only USPTO publication begins the submission period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents applicants from misusing the mechanism, avoids slowing prosecution with late third-party submissions after republication, and ensures USPTO publication triggers the submission window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retain Federal Circuit discretion over interlocutory claim-construction appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 8 omits provisions that would have created an expanded right to interlocutory appeals from claim-construction rulings and preserves the Federal Circuit's existing discretion to entertain such appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoids overwhelming the Federal Circuit and prevents easy removal of patent cases from district courts on interlocutory claim-construction grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental examination protection against inequitable-conduct attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 10 authorizes supplemental examination to present information not considered or inadequately considered; if the Office determines the information does not present a substantial new question of patentability or that the patent is still valid, that information cannot be used as a basis for an inequitable-conduct attack in civil litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure allows correction of errors or omissions before the Office; does not immunize misconduct—Office retains authority to sanction practitioners and to treat inequitable conduct/unenforceability consistent with existing doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office authority to sanction practitioner misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office has authority under section 32 of title 35 to bar an attorney from appearing before the Office for misconduct; existing regulations allow striking filings or reducing their weight; the Office has inherent authority to govern procedure and sanction attorneys for misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given these tools, there is no need to make courts supervise attorney conduct in Office proceedings; the bill extends statute of limitations for initiating such proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeal of Baldwin rule (Federal Circuit judge residency requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11 repeals the 'Baldwin rule' requiring Federal Circuit judges to live within 50 miles of Washington, D.C.; subsection (b) clarifies it does not require the Administrative Office of the Courts to provide facilities/support outside D.C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeal removes residency constraint while preserving AOC's existing authority regarding facilities and administrative support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best-mode requirement cannot be used to challenge priority/benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 15 adds a conforming subsection to ensure the best-mode requirement cannot be used to challenge a patent's entitlement to a right of priority or the benefit of an earlier filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Makes the change applicable to all proceedings commenced after enactment, including post-grant reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of deceptive-intent requirements for certain corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 16 reinserts language eliminating various deceptive-intent requirements related to correcting the naming of inventors, obtaining retroactive foreign filing licenses, seeking reissue, or enforcing remaining valid claims if a claim is invalidated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moves the U.S. patent system away from subjective-intent inquiries toward a more objective, evidence-based system that is cheaper to litigate and easier to administer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holmes Group 'fix' limiting state-court jurisdiction expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 17 enacts the so-called Holmes Group fix (H.R. 2955), abrogating Holmes Group to preclude state court jurisdiction over patent legal claims, but limits the bill’s expansion of Federal Circuit jurisdiction to only compulsory counterclaims asserting patent rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modifies prior proposals by limiting expansion to compulsory counterclaims (Rule 13(a)) rather than any counterclaim asserting patent rights.
